newsitem.title: USA: Clinton bans federal funding for human cloning.
newsitem.headline: Clinton bans federal funding for human cloning.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday banned federally funded human cloning and asked private scientists voluntarily to enact a similar moratorium while government advisers review the ethically troublesome issue.

The ban is broader than the prohibition on U.S.-funded human embryo research imposed in 1994, and Clinton said his intent was to close any loopholes pending the review of cloning he has requested from his National Bioethics Advisory Commission.

"My own view is that human cloning would have to raise deep concerns, given our most cherished concepts of faith and humanity. Each human life is unique, born of a miracle that reaches beyond laboratory science," Clinton said as he issued the executive directive from the Oval Office.

"I believe we must respect this profound gift and resist the temptation to replicate ourselves. At the very least, however, we should all agree that we need a better understanding of the scope and implications of this most recent breakthrough," he said.

The specter of making carbon copies of human beings crossed from the realm of science fiction to possible reality last week when a Scottish scientist introduced the world to Dolly, a lamb cloned from an adult sheep.
Although human cloning is not imminent, many scientists believe it will someday be technically possible -- though most term it morally repugnant.
Scientists do not worry that there will be a stampede to try to clone people, but they acknowledge the possibility of a renegade scientist daring such an attempt.
Ethicists generally have urged a cautious approach to the technology, which they regard as a watershed in the history of science comparable to splitting the atom.

"The process is working the way it should," said Harvard medical ethics expert Lisa Geller. "Scientists are putting it out in the public (for debate) ... Human cloning is nothing that someone is going to run out to do tomorrow."
Lawrence Gostin, a Georgetown University law professor who specialises in medical ethics, praised Clinton for doing "all that is within his power at the moment."

"He can't reach into the private sector, but it's extremely important that Congress follows up and reaches into the private sector," Gostin said. "It should be made unlawful and a voluntary ban is not enough."
Gostin also called on Clinton to begin a global movement to ban human cloning everywhere, much like international treaties seek to control nuclear and chemical weaponry.
Clinton conceded that cloning technology, applied to animals or human cells and proteins, could reap tremendous benefits for science, agriculture and medicine.
But echoing the ethical voices heard across the world since Dolly's debut, he said he was deeply troubled by the idea of cloning human beings.
"Any discovery that touches upon human creation is not simply a matter of scientific inquiry," he added. "It is a matter of morality and spirituality as well."
"We have a responsibility to move with caution and care to harness the powerful forces of science and technology so that we can reap the benefit while minimising the potential danger," he said.

Clinton has asked the National Bioethics Advisory Commission to review the legal and ethical issues involved and to report its findings within 90 days. The panel is headed by Princeton University president Harold Shapiro.
